title: Onion roots in two jars
body: A student placed one onion bulb each in two jars of water, Jar A and Jar B. She measured the length of the roots from the base of the bulb every day. For the first three days, the roots in both jars grew at about the same rate. On day 3, she cut about 1 cm from the tips of all the roots in Jar B and continued measuring for four more days. The roots in Jar A kept growing longer each day, while the roots in Jar B stopped increasing in length after the tips were cut. Earlier, under a microscope, she had seen many cells in different stages of mitosis in onion root tips.

title: Growing a carrot plant from single cells
body: In 1958, F. C. Steward took small fragments of phloem tissue from a carrot root and placed them in a liquid nutrient medium containing simple sugars and hormones. Stirring caused single cells to break free into the liquid. These single cells began to divide and formed a mass of unspecialised cells. Under suitable conditions, the mass divided further and formed an embryonic plant, which was moved to an agar medium and later planted in soil, where it grew into an adult carrot plant. In another set of trials, Steward changed light, air and the type of medium; the cells in a liquid medium with nutrients, given both light and air, showed about a 20 per cent increase in fresh weight, while cells on a solid medium showed reduced growth.
